definition: Simple Network Management Protocol — monitors and manages network devices (routers, switches). Use SNMPv3 for authentication + encryption; v1/v2c send community strings in plaintext.
Network Address Translation — translates private internal IPs to a public IP so many internal devices can share one internet-facing address.
Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol — automatically assigns IP addresses and network settings to devices. Rogue DHCP servers are a real threat; DHCP snooping on switches mitigates it.
New Technology File System — Windows' modern file system; supports per-user/group permissions (ACLs), encryption, and compression.
Encrypting File System — built into NTFS; encrypts individual files/folders tied to a user's certificate. Multiple authorized users' certificates can be added to one encrypted file.
Wi-Fi Protected Access — early-2000s wireless security standard using TKIP; replaced the broken WEP, later itself superseded by WPA2/WPA3.
Message Digest Algorithm 5 — 128-bit hash, cryptographically broken due to practical collision attacks. Don't use for security-sensitive integrity or signatures.
Pre-Shared Key — WPA-Personal mode where every device shares one passphrase. Hard to revoke access for a single user without rotating the key for everyone.
Secure Hash Algorithm — family (SHA-1/2/3) stronger than MD5. SHA-1 itself is now deprecated in favor of SHA-2/SHA-3.
Data Protection Officer — role (often required under GDPR) responsible for data protection compliance and acting as liaison with regulators and data subjects.
Wireless Transport Layer Security — lightweight, resource-constrained version of TLS built for early WAP-era mobile devices.
Protected EAP — wraps EAP authentication inside an encrypted TLS tunnel for secure 802.1X wireless authentication.
Lightweight EAP — older Cisco-proprietary wireless auth protocol; weak MS-CHAP-based exchange, vulnerable to offline dictionary attacks. Superseded by PEAP.
Security Content Automation Protocol — NIST standard for automating vulnerability management, configuration, and compliance checks using standardized, machine-readable formats.
Port-based network access control standard — requires authentication (often via RADIUS/EAP) before a device is granted network access. The basis of WPA-Enterprise.
Ticket-based network authentication protocol — uses a Key Distribution Center (KDC) to issue time-stamped tickets, avoiding transmission of plaintext passwords and resisting replay.
Mean Time Between Failures — average expected time between failures of a repairable system. Higher is better (more reliable).
Recovery Point Objective — the maximum acceptable amount of data loss, measured in time, which drives how often you must back up.
Mean Time To Repair — the average time it takes to fix/restore a failed system after a failure occurs.
Trusted Platform Module — hardware chip built into a device's motherboard; generates/stores cryptographic keys and supports full-disk encryption.
Giving a trusted third party a copy of a cryptographic key so it can be recovered if lost. Introduces its own compromise risk — whoever holds escrow becomes a high-value target.
International standard specifying requirements for an Information Security Management System (ISMS). This is the one organizations get formally certified against.
Companion standard to 27001 — describes the actual controls and practical guidance for implementing them. Not itself a certification standard.
Extension to ISO 27001 adding requirements/guidance for a Privacy Information Management System (PIMS) — covers PII handling and privacy obligations.
International standard providing general principles and guidelines for risk management — not security-specific, applies across any industry.

Infrastructure as a Service — you rent the raw infrastructure (servers, storage, networking) and manage the OS, apps, and data yourself. Like renting a kitchen and bringing your own dough and toppings.
Platform as a Service — the provider manages the OS/runtime platform; you manage your own apps and data. Like ordering the pizza but bringing your own table and drinks.
Software as a Service — the provider manages everything end-to-end; you just use the application. Like dining out — the restaurant handles it all.
Mandatory Access Control — the system enforces access based on centrally-assigned classification labels, not the resource owner's discretion. Military-style.
Discretionary Access Control — the resource owner decides who gets access. The most common model, e.g., Windows file permissions.
Role-Based Access Control — access is granted based on job role/group membership rather than per-user. Corporate style — everyone in "HR" gets HR access.
